entries.keywords: alphabet letters abc vowels consonants a e i o u
entries.a: The English alphabet has 26 letters. Five are vowels: a, e, i, o, u. The rest are consonants. Every word needs at least one vowel sound. Say each letter and its sound: a for apple, b for ball, c for cat.

entries.keywords: phonics sounds blending reading cvc words sound out
entries.a: Phonics means matching letters to sounds. To read cat, say the sounds c-a-t, then blend them together: cat. Practise with short words like sun, pen, dog, hat.

entries.keywords: sentence capital letter full stop complete sentence
entries.a: A sentence says a complete idea. It starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop (.), question mark (?) or exclamation mark (!). Example: The dog runs fast.

entries.keywords: noun verb adjective naming word action word describing word parts of speech
entries.a: A noun names a person, place or thing (girl, Harare, book). A verb is an action (jump, read). An adjective describes a noun (tall, green). In 'The tall girl reads a book', girl and book are nouns, reads is a verb and tall is an adjective.

entries.keywords: plural plurals singular more than one add s es children mice
entries.a: Plurals mean more than one. Usually add s: cat to cats. Add es after s, x, ch, sh: box to boxes. Change y to ies: baby to babies. Some are irregular: child to children, man to men, mouse to mice, foot to feet.

entries.keywords: tense tenses past present future verb ed will
entries.a: Tenses show when something happens. Present: I walk. Past: I walked. Future: I will walk. Many past tenses add -ed, but some are irregular: go to went, eat to ate, see to saw.

entries.keywords: punctuation comma apostrophe quotation marks speech marks colon
entries.a: Punctuation: a comma (,) separates items in a list. An apostrophe (') shows belonging (Tendai's bag) or a missing letter (don't). Speech marks go around the words someone says: "Good morning," said Mr Moyo.

entries.keywords: synonym antonym opposite same meaning homophone
entries.a: Synonyms mean nearly the same (big and large). Antonyms are opposites (hot and cold). Homophones sound the same but are spelt differently (see and sea, two and too).

entries.keywords: paragraph topic sentence essay writing structure composition
entries.a: A paragraph is a group of sentences about one idea. Start with a topic sentence, add details or examples, and end with a closing sentence. A composition has an introduction, body paragraphs and a conclusion. Plan first with a few notes.

entries.keywords: letter writing friendly letter formal letter address greeting yours sincerely
entries.a: A friendly letter has: your address, the date, a greeting (Dear Grace,), the body in paragraphs, and an ending (Yours lovingly, then your name). A formal letter also has the receiver's address, a subject line, and ends with 'Yours faithfully' if you do not know the name or 'Yours sincerely' if you do.

entries.keywords: comprehension reading passage questions answer understand
entries.a: For comprehension: read the passage twice, read the questions, then find the answer in the text. Answer in a full sentence using words from the question. For 'why' questions, include the word because. Underline the proof in the passage.

entries.keywords: simile metaphor figure of speech personification like as
entries.a: A simile compares using like or as: as brave as a lion. A metaphor says one thing is another: the classroom was a zoo. Personification gives human actions to things: the wind whispered.

entries.keywords: adverb adverbs quickly slowly how when where ly
entries.a: An adverb tells how, when or where an action happens: She walked slowly. We will go tomorrow. Many end in -ly (quickly, quietly).

entries.keywords: direct speech indirect speech reported speech narrative
entries.a: Direct speech gives the exact words: "I am tired," said Rudo. Indirect (reported) speech tells it without quoting: Rudo said that she was tired. The tense usually moves back one step and pronouns change.

entries.keywords: summary summarise main points precis short version
entries.a: To write a summary: read the passage, underline the main points, ignore examples and repetition, then write them in your own words in full sentences, keeping to the word limit.

entries.keywords: spelling tips i before e rule silent letters spell better
entries.a: Spelling tips: look, say, cover, write, check. Break long words into syllables (beau-ti-ful). Remember rules like 'i before e except after c' (receive, believe). Keep a list of words you get wrong and practise them.
